Because both **Sigmoid** and **Tanh** “flatten out” (saturate) at high and low input values, their derivatives become nearly zero.

In deep networks, multiplying these tiny numbers together during backpropagation caused the signal to disappear before it reached the earliest layers, a phenomenon known as the **vanishing gradient problem**.
The problem was diagnosed precisely in the early 1990s.

\citeauthor{hochreiter1991vanishing}'s \citeyear{hochreiter1991vanishing} diploma thesis analysed the repeated multiplication of Jacobians in backpropagation and showed that the error signal can shrink exponentially with depth; \cite[Bengio et al. (1994)]{bengio1994learning} made the result general and connected it to the difficulty of learning long-range dependencies.

The fix is not a single trick: ReLU keeps the derivative from vanishing on the active side, residual connections give the gradient a short path around a block, and gated recurrent architectures such as the LSTM and GRU learn to hold information across time.
The name "rectifier" comes from electronics: a half-wave rectifier passes the positive half of a signal and blocks the negative half, and $\max(0,x)$ is exactly that operation.

In the 2010 RBM experiments that brought it back, the rectified unit was not just a cheaper sigmoid; it changed the sparsity of the learned representations, with many units sitting exactly at zero \cite{relupaper}.
That sparsity is the subject of the next section.
The most common explanation for ReLU's success is that its derivative is 1 for positive inputs and 0 for negative ones, which prevents the vanishing gradient problem.
But there is a deeper insight: ReLU creates **sparsity**.
For any given input, roughly half of ReLU's neurons output exactly zero.
This means the network is effectively using a **different sparse subnetwork** for each input.
A neuron that activates for “dog” may be silent for “cat,” and vice versa.
Over the entire dataset, each neuron specializes in a subset of patterns, and every input activates only a fraction of the available neurons.

This connects directly to the \cite[Lottery Ticket Hypothesis]{frankle2019lottery}: within a large, randomly initialized network, there exist smaller subnetworks (“winning tickets”) that, when trained in isolation, can match the performance of the full network.
ReLU makes these subnetworks easier to find because its sparsity naturally partitions the network into overlapping but distinct computational pathways.
The “aha-moment”: ReLU doesn't just prevent vanishing gradients, it forces the network to use a different “team” of neurons for every input, creating **implicit specialization**.
No neuron needs to be a generalist; each can become an expert on a narrow pattern because it only fires when that pattern appears.

While ReLU became the workhorse of CNNs, the **Gaussian Error Linear Unit (GELU)**, introduced by \citeauthorlastnameand{hendrycks2016gelu} in \citeyear{hendrycks2016gelu}, became the standard activation in many **Transformer** feed-forward networks — GPT-1, BERT and their descendants — although the original Transformer used ReLU \cite{vaswani2017attention}.
This is the activation used in the FFN of the nanoGPT model we train in this course:
Where $\Phi(x)$ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function and $\text{erf}$ is the error function.
GELU is often described as a “smooth ReLU”: it behaves approximately like $\max(0, x)$ but is **everywhere differentiable** and keeps a small non-zero gradient for negative inputs.
This means the gradient is rarely exactly zero for negative inputs, so a detector can keep contributing a small signal during backpropagation.
It is this smoothness, combined with its superior performance on language modeling, that made GELU the natural choice for the Transformer's FFN.

The **Sigmoid Linear Unit (SiLU)** — introduced by \cite[Elfwing et al. (2017)]{elfwing2017silu} and independently found as **Swish** by \cite[Ramachandran et al. (2017)]{ramachandran2017swish} — is the activation inside the **U-Net denoiser of Stable Diffusion** \cite{rombach2022ldm} and in many modern vision models:
Both names describe the same self-gating trick: the input multiplies a gate that is a function of itself, so the unit can pass a signal, suppress it, or output a small negative value.

\cite[Elfwing et al. (2017)]{elfwing2017silu} approached it from reinforcement-learning value functions, while \cite[Ramachandran et al. (2017)]{ramachandran2017swish} found it by architecture search; the two papers arrived at the same curve from different directions.
That is a different mechanism from GELU's probabilistic gate, even though the two curves are nearly indistinguishable.
